We have yet to ﬁnd factors that affect the power-law exponent. To beat the power-law as we increase
data set size, models would need to learn more concepts with successively less data. In other words,
models must successively extract more marginal information from each additional training sample.
This might be difﬁcult without adjustments to the data set. We suggest that future work more deeply
analyze learning curves when using data handling techniques, such as data ﬁltering/augmentation,
few-shot learning, experience replay, and generative adversarial networks.

Figure 3.5: Zero-, one-, and few-shot performance on the adversarial Winogrande dataset as model capacity scales.
Scaling is relatively smooth with the gains to few-shot learning increasing with model size, and few-shot GPT-3 175B
is competitive with a ﬁne-tuned RoBERTA-large.

Second, we train our models on random subsets of 9M, 30M, and 90M as well as the full JFT-
300M dataset. We do not perform additional regularization on the smaller subsets and use the same
hyper-parameters for all settings. This way, we assess the intrinsic model properties, and not the
effect of regularization. We do, however, use early-stopping, and report the best validation accuracy
achieved during training. To save compute, we report few-shot linear accuracy instead of full ﬁne-
tuning accuracy. Figure 4 contains the results. Vision Transformers overﬁt more than ResNets with
comparable computational cost on smaller datasets. For example, ViT-B/32 is slightly faster than
ResNet50; it performs much worse on the 9M subset, but better on 90M+ subsets. The same is true
for ResNet152x2 and ViT-L/16. This result reinforces the intuition that the convolutional inductive
bias is useful for smaller datasets, but for larger ones, learning the relevant patterns directly from
data is sufﬁcient, even beneﬁcial.

In this paper, we test this hypothesis by training a 175 billion parameter autoregressive language model, which we call
GPT-3, and measuring its in-context learning abilities. Speciﬁcally, we evaluate GPT-3 on over two dozen NLP datasets,
as well as several novel tasks designed to test rapid adaptation to tasks unlikely to be directly contained in the training
set. For each task, we evaluate GPT-3 under 3 conditions: (a) “few-shot learning”, or in-context learning where we
allow as many demonstrations as will ﬁt into the model’s context window (typically 10 to 100), (b) “one-shot learning”,
where we allow only one demonstration, and (c) “zero-shot” learning, where no demonstrations are allowed and only
an instruction in natural language is given to the model. GPT-3 could also in principle be evaluated in the traditional
ﬁne-tuning setting, but we leave this to future work.

Metrics. We report results on downstream datasets either through few-shot or ﬁne-tuning accuracy.
Fine-tuning accuracies capture the performance of each model after ﬁne-tuning it on the respective
dataset. Few-shot accuracies are obtained by solving a regularized least-squares regression problem
that maps the (frozen) representation of a subset of training images to {−1, 1}K target vectors. This
formulation allows us to recover the exact solution in closed form. Though we mainly focus on
ﬁne-tuning performance, we sometimes use linear few-shot accuracies for fast on-the-ﬂy evaluation
where ﬁne-tuning would be too costly.

LAMBADA is also a demonstration of the ﬂexibility of few-shot learning as it provides a way to address a problem that
classically occurs with this dataset. Although the completion in LAMBADA is always the last word in a sentence, a
standard language model has no way of knowing this detail. It thus assigns probability not only to the correct ending but
also to other valid continuations of the paragraph. This problem has been partially addressed in the past with stop-word
ﬁlters [RWC+19] (which ban “continuation” words). The few-shot setting instead allows us to “frame” the task as a
cloze-test and allows the language model to infer from examples that a completion of exactly one word is desired. We
use the following ﬁll-in-the-blank format:

For VTAB we follow the protocol in Kolesnikov et al. (2020), and use the same hyperparameter
setting for all tasks. We use a learning rate of 0.01 and train for 2500 steps (Tab. 4). We chose this
setting by running a small sweep over two learning rates and two schedules, and selecting the setting
with the highest VTAB score on the 200-example validation sets. We follow the pre-processing used
in Kolesnikov et al. (2020), except that we do not use task-speciﬁc input resolutions. Instead we ﬁnd
that Vision Transformer beneﬁts most from a high resolution (384 × 384) for all tasks.

We ﬁrst discuss emergent abilities in the prompting paradigm, as pop-
ularized by GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020).2 In prompting, a pre-trained
language model is given a prompt (e.g. a natural language instruction)
of a task and completes the response without any further training
or gradient updates to its parameters. Brown et al. (2020) proposed
few-shot prompting, which includes a few input-output examples in
the model’s context (input) as a preamble before asking the model to
perform the task for an unseen inference-time example. An example prompt is shown in Figure 1.

On Winograd we test GPT-3 on the original set of 273 Winograd schemas, using the same “partial evaluation” method
described in [RWC+19]. Note that this setting differs slightly from the WSC task in the SuperGLUE benchmark, which
is presented as binary classiﬁcation and requires entity extraction to convert to the form described in this section. On
Winograd GPT-3 achieves 88.3%, 89.7%, and 88.6% in the zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot settings, showing no clear
in-context learning but in all cases achieving strong results just a few points below state-of-the-art and estimated human
performance. We note that contamination analysis found some Winograd schemas in the training data but this appears
to have only a small effect on results (see Section 4).

## Few-shot learning

Across this corpus of ~100 research papers, "few-shot learning" is treated most authoritatively in the GPT-3 paper, and appears in three distinct roles: (1) as a formally defined *in-context learning* setting, (2) as an *evaluation protocol* for representation quality, and (3) as an *emergent ability* of scale. Here is the synthesis, with every claim cited to document and page.

### 1. The canonical definition (in-context, no weight updates)

The primary source is **`2005.14165` — "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (GPT-3)**. It defines Few-Shot (FS) as one of four points on a spectrum of how much task-specific data a model relies on (Fine-Tuning → Few-Shot → One-Shot → Zero-Shot):

- **Few-shot** is "the setting where the model is given a few demonstrations of the task at inference time as conditioning, but **no weight updates are allowed**." The model is shown *K* (context, completion) example pairs, then a final context, and is expected to produce the completion. *K* is typically **10 to 100**, bounded by what fits in the context window (n_ctx = 2048) (`2005.14165`, p. 6).
- Framed another way: few-shot is "in-context learning where we allow as many demonstrations as will fit into the model's context window (typically 10 to 100)," as opposed to **one-shot** (exactly one demonstration) and **zero-shot** (only a natural-language instruction, no demonstrations) (`2005.14165`, p. 5).
- **Advantages / disadvantages:** it sharply reduces the need for task-specific data and avoids overfitting a narrow fine-tuning distribution; but at the time results were "much worse than state-of-the-art fine-tuned models," and a small amount of task-specific data is still required (`2005.14165`, p. 6).
- **Relationship to classical few-shot learning:** the authors explicitly connect it to few-shot learning as used elsewhere in ML — "both involve learning based on a broad distribution of tasks (in this case implicit in the pre-training data) and then rapidly adapting to a new task" (`2005.14165`, p. 6). This meta-learning framing recurs: the gap between zero-, one-, and few-shot performance tends to grow with model capacity, "perhaps suggesting that larger models are more proficient meta-learners" (`2005.14165`, p. 6).

Concrete illustrations of the payoff in that paper:
- On **LAMBADA**, few-shot lets the task be reframed as a cloze test so the model infers that a single-word completion is desired — a flexibility a plain language model lacks (`2005.14165`, p. 12).
- On **Winograd**, GPT-3 scores 88.3 / 89.7 / 88.6% in zero-/one-/few-shot — strong, though here showing "no clear in-context learning" (`2005.14165`, p. 17).

### 2. Few-shot as an evaluation protocol (vision)

In **`2010.11929` — the Vision Transformer (ViT) paper**, "few-shot" denotes a concrete, cheap *measurement method* rather than a prompting paradigm:
- Few-shot accuracies are obtained "by solving a regularized least-squares regression problem that maps the (frozen) representation of a subset of training images to {−1, 1}^K target vectors," recoverable in closed form — used for "fast on-the-fly evaluation where fine-tuning would be too costly" (`2010.11929`, p. 5).
- Using **few-shot linear accuracy** on JFT-300M subsets (9M/30M/90M/full), they show ViT overfits more than ResNets on small data but overtakes them on larger data — evidence that the convolutional inductive bias helps mostly on smaller datasets (`2010.11929`, p. 7).

### 3. Few-shot prompting as an emergent ability of scale

**`2206.07682` — "Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models"** treats few-shot prompting as the paradigm GPT-3 popularized: "a pre-trained language model is given a prompt... and completes the response without any further training or gradient updates," with a few input-output examples included in context as a preamble (`2206.07682`, p. 3). The paper notes that features of the pre-training data (long-range coherence, many rare classes) correlate with **emergent** few-shot prompting, that it "can require certain model architectures in some scenarios," and points to work on improving general few-shot prompting abilities (`2206.07682`, p. 8).

### 4. Supporting / peripheral mentions

- **`2203.15556` (Chinchilla)** reports few-shot benchmark numbers, e.g. RACE-m 86.8 and RACE-h 82.3 in the few-shot setting (`2203.15556`, p. 12), and cites GPT-3 as "Language models are few-shot learners" (p. 17).
- **`1712.00409` (deep-learning scaling / power-law study)** lists few-shot learning as future work — a data-handling technique worth analyzing to "beat the power-law" as dataset size grows (`1712.00409`, p. 12).
- Reference-only citations to the GPT-3 / Flamingo few-shot literature appear in **`2205.14135` (FlashAttention)** p. 11, **`2010.14701`** p. 36, **`2312.00752` (Mamba)** p. 18, and **`2605.06546`** pp. 11–12 (the last citing Flamingo, "a visual language model for few-shot learning," and a "framework for few-shot language model evaluation").

### Bottom line

In this corpus, **few-shot learning** most precisely means: *conditioning a frozen (pre-trained) model on a small number K of task demonstrations (~10–100) at inference time, with no weight updates, so it rapidly adapts to a new task* — the definition set out in the GPT-3 paper (`2005.14165`, pp. 5–6). Two important nuances the corpus adds: in vision (ViT) "few-shot" often refers specifically to a cheap linear-probe accuracy on frozen features (`2010.11929`, p. 5), and the prompting form of few-shot is characterized as an *emergent ability* that appears with sufficient model scale and the right pre-training data (`2206.07682`, pp. 3, 8).
